title: Adaptive sequence-length thermostat runner and control-plane reporter
author: Maya Chen
description: Motivation: Real workloads at Redwood show sequence-length drift over time which causes p95 latency violations even when average token rates are within SLO. This PR introduces an adaptive "thermostat" style workload runner that dynamically adjusts the incoming sequence-length mix during a run, coupled with a small control-plane reporter that emits control signals and latency feedback to the benchmark pipeline. Goals: 1) provide a representative closed-loop workload that mimics production sequence-length shifts; 2) allow us to stress routing and batching heuristics to test latency SLO stability; 3) surface a compact telemetry artifact (control signals + latency envelope) consumable by downstream regression detectors. What this PR adds: - benchmark_lab/runners/thermostat_runner.py: a Python-based runner that reads an initial sequence-length distribution, target p95, and step policy; it measures instantaneous p95 over sliding windows and adjusts the sequence mix up/down to steer toward the target. - reports/latency_thermostat_reporter.go: a lightweight reporter that aggregates latency histograms, emits control commands (scale up long sequences / reduce long sequences) and writes a compact JSON timeline for the pipeline. - ci/benchmark-pipeline.yml: a pipeline stage to run thermostat experiments and upload timelines to S3 for downstream analysis. - docs/bench/thermostat-runner.md: rationale, configuration flags, and examples for reproducing experiments. - tests/integration/test_thermostat_runner.py: harness-level tests that validate thermostat stability under synthetic distributions. Design notes: the runner uses a PID-lite controller (proportional + integral window) to avoid oscillation; adjustments are applied as fractional swaps between sequence-length buckets rather than generating brand new sequences to keep dataset locality stable. We intentionally keep the reporter implementation minimal: reporter emits epoch-level summaries and a single timeline artifact; downstream jobs can ingest that to compute regression deltas. How to run locally: python -m benchmark_lab.runners.thermostat_runner --config examples/thermostat/short-to-long.json --target-p95 180 --duration 900 Checks and results: I ran the standard bench-suite, unit-tests, lint and the new integration harness. A few iterations of PID tuning were required after reviewer feedback to avoid slow oscillation. The final run on our internal k8s staging cluster showed the runner successfully holding p95 within +/-5% of target across 15m windows while increasing long-sequence ratio from 10% to 40% over the run. Migration/compatibility: non-breaking; runner lives under benchmark_lab/runners and is opt-in. Checklist: - [x] Implementation - [x] Unit/integration tests - [x] CI pipeline - [x] Docs - [x] Bench artifacts uploaded to S3 Related: this work complements ENG-6120 (seq-mix profiling) and is intended to feed datasets into the latency-regression detector.

review_comments: Arjun: Overall nice design. Two requests: reduce the default integral window to avoid slow oscillation and add an option to cap per-step swap fraction.
Maya: Reduced integral window from 10 to 4 epochs, added --max-swap-fraction flag and unit tests.
Lina: Can we make the reporter emit cold-start markers so we can correlate init spikes? Added markers in epoch metadata.
Tomás: Integration test is flaky on CI (timing). Switched to simulated time in test harness; reran pipeline.
release_notes: Added an adaptive thermostat workload runner and a compact latency control-plane reporter. New benchmark experiments can simulate sequence-length drift and produce timeline artifacts for regression detection.
